models.name: Bayes lookahead
models.tagline: Counts every card it has seen and picks the move with the lowest expected final score. No tunable parameters.
how: Keeps an exact belief over the cards it hasn't seen yet: all 52 cards start unseen, and every face-up card, discard and its own held card is crossed off as it appears.
Scores a layout by its expected final score, treating each face-down slot as a draw without replacement from the unseen cards, including the exact chance that a column pairs up.

Stage 1: tries the held card in all six slots and keeps the best placement if it beats the current expected score. Otherwise it discards and flips, since flipping a card changes the variance but not the expected score.
Stage 0: compares taking the known discard with drawing, averaging the draw over all 13 ranks weighted by how many of each are still unseen.
strengths: Best agent in the repo on both score and win rate.
A scramble test confirms it never peeks at hidden cards.
weaknesses: Ignores opponents: it doesn't model when someone is about to end the hole.

models.name: DQN champion
models.tagline: A self-attention Q-network trained by population self-play over 350 generations. The strongest learned agent.
how: Model v3 (GolfDQNv3) embeds each card as rank plus suit, runs a Transformer encoder over the card tokens so it can compare ranks across slots for column matches, then pools them into an MLP that outputs Q-values for the 16 actions.
Trained by population-based DQN in src/tournament.py: 8 agents train in parallel through vectorized self-play, play a round-robin each generation, and the best survive and mutate.
Uses hindsight reward shaping and cyclic epsilon annealing (350 generations in 7 cycles of 50). The champion is Exp 14, generation 350, agent 4.
strengths: Beats both hand-coded heuristics by a wide margin.
Learned to swap out face-up cards and build column matches by itself.
weaknesses: About 0.5 points per hole behind the lookahead.
Needs PyTorch and a checkpoint, so it can't run in the browser yet.

models.name: Improved heuristic
models.tagline: The base heuristic plus one change: it will also replace cards that are already face-up.
how: Stage 0: takes the discard if it's worth less than 4 points or matches the rank of one of its face-up cards. Otherwise it draws.

Stage 1: tries the held card in all six slots. If the best spot saves at least 4 points it places it there. If not, and the move doesn't make things worse by 4 or more, it places it on the first face-down slot. Otherwise it discards and flips.
strengths: Swapping out face-up cards alone takes the base heuristic from about 14 to about 10.5 points per hole against the same opponents.
weaknesses: Fixed thresholds: it doesn't count cards, so it can't tell when the deck is rich or poor in low cards.

models.name: Base heuristic
models.tagline: The original rule-based player and the RL baseline. Column-aware, but it never touches a face-up card.
how: Stage 0: same as the improved heuristic. It takes the discard if it's worth less than 4 points or matches a face-up rank, otherwise it draws.
Stage 1: only considers face-down slots, using the same 4-point thresholds to decide between placing and discard-and-flip.
strengths: Imitation learning reproduces it exactly, which makes it the reference point for RL.
weaknesses: Never replaces a bad face-up card, which costs about 3.5 points per hole compared with the improved version.

models.name: Greedy
models.tagline: Takes low discards and puts every card on a random face-down slot. A sanity check that sits between random and the heuristics.
how: Stage 0: takes the discard if it's worth less than 4 points, otherwise draws.
Stage 1: always places the held card, on a random face-down slot (or any slot once all are face-up).
strengths: Shows how much of the heuristics' edge comes from simply keeping low cards.
weaknesses: No column matching and no card counting. It even places high cards.

models.name: Random
models.tagline: Picks uniformly among legal moves. The floor every other agent is measured against.
how: Stage 0: takes or draws with equal probability.
Stage 1: picks uniformly among all legal placements and flips.
strengths: Gives a fixed reference point for every benchmark.

models.name: claude-haiku-4.5
models.tagline: A hosted language model playing from a text description of the table. It beats random easily but mostly loses to the base heuristic.
how: src/llm_player.py renders the game state as a text prompt, parses the model's reply into an action and checks it against the legal moves.
Played through OpenRouter in the seats LLM, Random, Heuristic, Random: 5 matches of 9 holes.
strengths: Zero invalid actions across all runs.
Beats random by about 14 points per hole.
weaknesses: Lost to the base heuristic in 4 of 5 matches.
Almost never builds column matches, and very often replaces face-up cards (about 78% of placements).

models.name: deepseek-r1-7b
models.tagline: A small local reasoning model. It thinks at length but plays at about random level.
how: Run locally through LM Studio with the same LLM harness, stateless prompts and up to 4,096 output tokens per move.
One 9-hole match took about three hours because each move averaged roughly 1,700 reasoning tokens.
strengths: Takes the discard often, so it does try to use known cards.
weaknesses: 15% of its moves were invalid even after the prompt fixes.
